entry.evidence: However, such a framework has been lacking to describe the evolution of the outer circulation.

steps.action: The authors pose the question of how tropical cyclone outer size evolves, noting that size evolution has received little attention compared with size climatology and environmental controls.
steps.quote: the size evolution itself has received relatively less attention

steps.action: The authors take from Schenkel et al. (2018) basin differences in growth duration, growth rate, initial size and LMS, and note that these rest only on reanalysis and climate-model data.
steps.quote: These findings were however only based on reanalysis and climate model data.

steps.action: The authors state the model premises: gradient wind balance at the top of the boundary layer, and a small, quasi-stationary mean effective inflow angle following a fixed-wind radius. Gradient balance is supported by cited flight observations.
steps.quote: The model is established on the assumption that at the top of a TC boundary layer the flow is in gradient wind balance

steps.action: The authors derive the analytic growth model. They start from the axisymmetric angular momentum budget, transform coordinates to follow R_V, and scale-analyse the terms using a modified Rankine vortex and cited scales (Table 2). This yields exponential growth (Eq. 9) with time constant f_o times the mean inflow angle, and a doubling time (Eq. 10).
steps.quote: Equation (9) is the full expression of a new analytic solution for TC outer size growth.

steps.action: The authors run a 9-day full-physics WRF idealized TC simulation (triple nest, 4-km inner grid, constant 27 °C SST, stationary environment) to test the model and the steady inflow-angle assumption.
steps.quote: To validate the growth model and examine the steady-state inflow angle assumption we perform idealized TC simulations.

steps.action: The authors fit Eq. 9 by least squares to the simulated R34 growth, with a wind adjustment factor of 0.75 (r = 0.99), and infer a mean effective inflow angle of 1.0°.
steps.quote: From the fit we infer a mean effective inflow angle

steps.action: The authors compare the inferred inflow angle with the simulated inflow angle following R34 and find it at about 1500 m, the top of the boundary layer.
steps.quote: this mean effective inflow angle is seen in the simulation at a height of about 1500 m

steps.action: The authors check the model premises in the simulation. The inflow angle shows no significant change during growth, and the simulated wind adjustment factor (0.76) is close to the assumed 0.75.
steps.quote: We do not find a statistically significant (P value > 0.05) change of the inflow angle during the growth period in this simulation

steps.action: The authors assemble IBTrACS best-track R34 for 2004–2017 (NHC for NA and EP, JTWC for the other basins). They filter out extratropical transition, land records and short records, and composite R34 for 48 h before the LMS.
steps.quote: We next validate the growth model by compositing the TC outer size

steps.action: The authors compare the observed composite, which grows super-linearly with increasing 6-h increments, with the exponential growth predicted by the model.
steps.quote: This is qualitatively in line with the prediction by the exponential growth model.

steps.action: The authors fit Eq. 9 to each NA and EP storm. Initial size, duration and mean latitude are observed inputs; the inflow angle is a free parameter per storm. Correlation with observed R34 is r = 0.93 (NA) and 0.90 (EP), with slopes below one.
steps.quote: is treated as a fitting parameter for each TC

steps.action: The authors vary the inputs: the basin-mean f_o and mean R_o replace per-storm values via partial correlation, and the wind adjustment factor is varied between 0.7 and 1.0 (Methods). The fits are reported as essentially unchanged.
steps.quote: Partial correlation analysis reveals that correlation coefficient in Fig. 3 does not change if the mean fo is used for all TCs

steps.action: The authors test log-transformed LMS and initial size for normality with KS tests: LMS is lognormal, initial size much less so. They compare NA and EP growth factors by bootstrapping; LMS, initial size, duration and latitude differ significantly, and the inflow angle differs at P = 0.04.
steps.quote: This means the distribution of LMS in these two basins has a strong lognormal feature.

steps.action: The authors apply the growth-model fit to storms in all six basins, using JTWC data for WP, NI, SI and SP. Global r = 0.83, basin range 0.80–0.87, RMSE 24 km.
steps.quote: The global correlation coefficient is 0.83, with variation between 0.80 and 0.87 in all the basins

steps.action: The authors compare each basin's growth factors with those of all other basins by bootstrapping (Table 5) and explain each basin's distinctive LMS by its combination of factors.
steps.quote: There are different reasons for the uniqueness of LMS in these basins

steps.action: The authors compute each storm's LMS with Eq. 9 from its observed factors and compare the modeled annual median LMS with the observed series (detrended r = 0.86). The observed series shows no significant trend.
steps.quote: The correlation between the modeled and observed annual LMS time series is 0.86 after detrending

steps.action: The authors run sensitivity experiments that fix each growth factor in turn to its global median. They conclude that growth duration most consistently drives interannual LMS variation, and that latitude contributes little.
steps.quote: [...] next perform sensitivity experiments by fixing each of the four growth factors to their global medians

steps.action: The authors set the model against prior empirical findings: the role of initial size, the increase of size with latitude, inter-basin size differences, and lognormal size distributions. They claim the model unifies them.
steps.quote: The model also explains several empirical findings into a single framework

steps.action: The authors use the model with global mean factors and a 1-day shortening of major-TC duration, taken from their own earlier work (ref. 40), to predict the change in mean LMS over 37 years.
steps.quote: the growth model predicts a reduction of mean LMS by −53 km over 37 years

steps.action: The authors compare the predicted −1.4 km per year with a published best-track R34 trend of −2.5 km per year, with satellite studies reporting no change, and with their own earlier cold-wake inference of steady R34.
steps.quote: This predicted change is close to an observed value in a recent study41

steps.action: The authors report an unshown sensitivity test of LMS to growth latitude: a 50% latitude increase raises LMS by less than 10%.
steps.quote: further analysis (not shown) reveals that the growth model is the least sensitive to any latitude change

steps.action: The authors compare their inferred inflow angle (1.0°) with an independent estimate of about 1.8° derived from Zhang et al. (2011) boundary-layer observations at R34.
steps.quote: The magnitude of this inferred top-of-boundary-layer inflow angle agrees with our estimates from simulations (1.0°)

steps.action: The authors invoke the law of proportionate effect (Central Limit Theorem), taken from statistics, to explain why exponential growth makes the LMS lognormal while the initial size is not.
steps.quote: The exponential growth model is essentially an expression of the law of proportionate effect

steps.action: The authors retain the analytic exponential growth model as describing modeled and observed outer-size growth, together with its four growth factors.
steps.quote: The analytic growth model can capture the size growth of both modeled and observed individual storm events.

tree.answer: Growth of TC outer size (R34) from first record to lifetime maximum; known to grow, but no framework for its evolution
R34 is observed in best track; the mean effective inflow angle is latent and inferred by fitting
Derive an analytic growth model and validate it on a simulation and on observations
No stated rival model; only an implicit contrast with linear growth (super-linear composite)
Exponential (super-linear) growth, inflow angle near 1° at boundary-layer top, lognormal LMS
Conditions set in one idealized WRF run; conditions found in best-track storms

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Nature repeats: 549 storms across six basins, 2004–2017
Fits robust to mean f_o and R_o and to wind adjustment factor 0.7–1.0; holds in all basins
Model kept as a regularity with stated factors

end.claim: TC outer-size (R34) growth from first record to lifetime maximum follows an analytic exponential law with time constant f_o times the mean effective inflow angle. It fits an idealized simulation and best-track storms in all six basins (2004–2017), controlled by initial size, growth duration, latitude and inflow angle.

decisive_move.sentence: Deriving Eq. (9) from the angular momentum budget by coordinate transformation and scale analysis creates the exponential growth law that every later fit and comparison tests.

gates.evidence: Action: the derived model directed the WRF simulation, run 'To validate the growth model and examine the steady-state inflow angle assumption' (§4.2 ¶1). The best-track data were archival and not acquired for the hypothesis. Claim: the composite could have been sub-linear, and the inflow angle inferred from the fit could have mismatched the simulated angle at the boundary-layer top (§2.2 ¶16, §2.3 ¶1). The observational fits, however, leave one free inflow-angle parameter per storm, so high r is partly built in (inference). Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Law of proportionate effect and Central Limit Theorem, generating lognormal distributions (Limpert et al., BioScience; Aitchison & Brown, economics)
Kolmogorov–Smirnov normality test and bootstrap resampling for significance of distribution differences
Doubling time of an exponential growth process

novelty_claims.quote: formulating the first growth model of TC outer size
Equation (9) is the full expression of a new analytic solution for TC outer size growth.
A simple analytic model for TC outer size growth has been lacking.

limits: No review file, discussion or earlier version was supplied, so only the final-paper sequence is coded. No rival growth model (e.g. linear growth, or a model with an equilibrium size) is fitted against the exponential one, so 'supports exponential growth' rests on super-linearity and fit quality. In the observational fits the inflow angle is a free parameter per storm and initial size and duration are taken from the data; high correlations are therefore partly expected by construction (inference). The independent constraint on the inflow angle is one WRF run plus one literature estimate (1.8° vs 1.0°). The text gives the simulated mean inflow angle as 1.0°, the Figure 1 caption as 1.1°. The latitude sensitivity is 'not shown'. Code is available only on request. Best-track R34 uncertainty is large (25–35% in NA, unknown in EP; JTWC mostly real-time), and the authors call this the main uncertainty, without propagating it into the fits. The model assumes axisymmetry and cannot describe R34 decay or a maximum size. Sub-claims and their statuses: the inflow angle of about 1° at the top of the boundary layer (estimate_with_resolution, with no uncertainty given); the inter-basin LMS differences explained by factor combinations (best_explanation); the lognormal LMS explained by the law of proportionate effect (best_explanation); growth duration as the main driver of interannual LMS variability (best_explanation, from one-at-a-time fixing; the authors write 'may be'); the projected −1.4 km per year LMS change (an illustrative estimate, not tested).

disagreements.target: Schenkel et al. (2018), lifetime evolution of outer TC size from reanalysis and climate model data
disagreements.support: The paper re-examines basin differences in growth with best-track R34 observations rather than reanalysis, and explains them with its growth model.
disagreements.quote: These findings were however only based on reanalysis and climate model data.

disagreements.target: Chavas & Emanuel (2010) and Dean et al. (2009): TC size lognormal only after normalization by potential intensity / Coriolis [...]
disagreements.support: KS tests show unnormalized LMS is lognormal in NA and EP. The paper reconciles this with prior work by noting that earlier climatologies pooled all lifecycle sizes.
disagreements.quote: This is not contradictory to the previous study12 since their size climatology covered all sizes during a lifecycle.
